title: A Bell for the Choir
premise: Isandro Dunmore, a property surveyor, is hired to appraise the Harrow house in the town of Vell's Crossing and moves in to complete the assessment. The house answers questions asked aloud during Isandro's sleep recordings—a second voice that knows things no one should know, including the fates of every family who has lived there. As Isandro digs into the town archives, they learn the voice belongs to a child drowned by the founding families in 1891, kept alive as the house's 'count': every household must surrender a member or be taken whole. The neighboring Aldous family is next on the count, and Isandro—having spent twenty years making themselves invisible after testifying against a corrupt employer cost an innocent man everything—must choose between staying safe and forcing the town to finally answer for its bargain. In the end, Isandro breaks the count not by destroying the house but by giving it what it actually wants: a public reckoning, reading the founders' names and crimes aloud until the voice, satisfied, lets the house go quiet—and takes Isandro's own name off the ledger at a price they accept.
about_author: Wendell Eastwick is the pen name of a former county records clerk who spent eleven years cataloguing deeds, easements, and probate files in rural New England. Their fiction draws on the paperwork of small towns—the ledgers where old debts are quietly forgotten.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Isandro Dunmore. Isandro arrives in Vell's Crossing to appraise the Harrow house, noting its impossible measurements—a hallway longer inside than out. They meet the nervous Aldous family next door. Emotional beat: professional detachment masking twenty years of practiced invisibility.

chapters.title: Settling In
chapters.summary: Isandro moves into the empty house for the two-week assessment. Small wrongnesses accumulate: doors found open, cold spots, a child's chalk hopscotch grid on the cellar floor dated 1891. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: rationalization as survival habit—we see how good they've become at explaining things away.

chapters.title: Baseline Noise
chapters.summary: To document defects for the report, Isandro sets up overnight audio recorders. The first night captures settling sounds, pipes, wind. The second night captures footsteps that stop outside their bedroom door and wait. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: dread arriving through the most mundane instrument.

chapters.title: Questions in Sleep
chapters.summary: Reviewing recordings, Isandro hears themselves talking in their sleep—and a second voice answering. It responds only to direct questions, and its answers are precise: dates, names, causes of death. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery curdling into horror when the voice says, unprompted, 'You ask like the last one did.'

chapters.title: The Ledger Room
chapters.summary: Following the voice's hints, Isandro finds a sealed room behind the pantry wall containing a ledger listing every household in Vell's Crossing since 1891, each with a name struck through. The Aldous family's page is fresh-inked. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: the shift from haunted-house curiosity to moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Knows
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Ruth Aldous, who has lived beside the house her whole life. She recognizes what Isandro has found and begs them to stop looking, revealing fragments: the town pays a tithe, always has, and asking questions marks you. Emotional beat: complicity and fear; she loves her town and hates what it costs.

chapters.title: Drowned in the Cistern
chapters.summary: In the town archive, Isandro finds the 1891 record: a child, Wren Harrow, drowned in the cistern beneath the house while six founding families watched—punishment for her father's refusal to join their land scheme. The house was built over her. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: grief and fury braided together.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: The voice explains itself fully in a recorded session: the founders bound it to keep the town prosperous, but the binding requires a count—one soul per generation, chosen by the house. It does not want to take anyone. It wants to be released. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: sympathy for the monster; the horror reframed as injustice.

chapters.title: Twenty Years Invisible
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter. Isandro remembers testifying about their employer's falsified safety reports, the whistleblower who took the fall, and the years since spent never signing anything, never staying anywhere, never being counted. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: the theme crystallizes—invisibility was survival, but also surrender.

chapters.title: First Mark
chapters.summary: Isandro's own name appears in the ledger, inked faintly. The house has noticed them. That night the voice asks a question back for the first time: 'Will you help me?' POV Isandro. Emotional beat: exposure—the invisible person made visible, hunted by a house.

chapters.title: The Town That Looks Away
chapters.summary: Isandro confronts the town councilman, Emeric Vell, descendant of the founders. He is polite, offers money, then threats, revealing the count is administered knowingly by a handful of families who keep everyone else ignorant. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: power's banality; corruption wearing a cardigan.

chapters.title: Ruth's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Ruth. She confesses her own debt: thirty years ago she gave the house her sister's name to save her son. Her guilt has calcified into silence. Now the count circles her grandchildren. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid across decades, love twisted into betrayal.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: Isandro experiments with the recordings, learning the voice can act—moving objects, opening the sealed room—but only within the house, and only when named aloud. They realize the binding's mechanism: the founders' oath, read aloud, holds it. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: hope with teeth; a plan forming.

chapters.title: Evasion
chapters.summary: Vell's men break into the house to retrieve the ledger. Isandro escapes through the too-long hallway as the house itself seems to mislead the intruders—staircases reversing, rooms refusing. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: terror and a strange alliance; the house protecting them.

chapters.title: The Other Families
chapters.summary: Isandro tracks down descendants of the six founders. One, ancient and dying, confirms everything and gives them the original oath text—then warns that breaking the count unbinds the house's prosperity too. Vell's Crossing will rot. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: the true cost revealed; justice versus the common good.

chapters.title: Ruth Decides
chapters.summary: POV Ruth. She finds her granddaughter's name freshly inked in a copy of the ledger Vell keeps at the church. She burns it, knowing there will be consequences, and goes to Isandro: 'Tell me what you need.' Emotional beat: redemption chosen late; courage as a decision, not a feeling.

chapters.title: Preparations
chapters.summary: Isandro and Ruth plan a public reading of the founders' oath and crimes at the harvest gathering, where the whole town attends. The voice tells them the count falls tomorrow night. They copy the ledger pages as evidence. POV alternating. Emotional beat: grim resolve; two broken people arming themselves with paper.

chapters.title: Harvest Night
chapters.summary: At the gathering, Vell recognizes them and has Isandro seized before they can speak. Ruth reads anyway, voice shaking, naming the founders and Wren Harrow before the crowd. The lights fail. Every recording device in town begins playing the drowned child's voice. POV alternating. Emotional beat: climax ignites; truth spoken aloud cannot be re-swallowed.

chapters.title: The Reckoning
chapters.summary: The house opens—doors standing wide, the cistern exposed, Wren's remains visible to all. The founders' descendants are compelled toward it by something older than the oath. Vell, dragged last, screams confessions the whole town hears. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: cathartic horror; justice arriving outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: The Price
chapters.summary: The voice appears to Isandro one final time: the binding is broken, but a count was begun, and it must close. It offers a choice—it will take Isandro's name instead of the Aldous child's. Isandro, who spent twenty years avoiding being counted, agrees freely. POV Isandro. Emotional beat: sacrifice as authorship; reclaiming agency through loss.

chapters.title: Quiet House
chapters.summary: POV Ruth, weeks later. The Harrow house stands ordinary, sold at fair value, its measurements correct. The town is poorer and somehow more honest. Ruth visits Isandro once—they are changed, diminished, but alive, having traded years rather than their life. Emotional beat: bittersweet aftermath; survival redefined.

chapters.title: A Bell for the Choir
chapters.summary: Final chapter, POV Isandro. They stay in Vell's Crossing, sign their name on a lease—the first signature in twenty years—and hang a small bell in the repaired church tower, ringing it for Wren and for everyone the ledger swallowed. Some nights, faintly, a second bell answers. Emotional beat: peace without forgetting; being counted, at last, on one's own terms.
